content: Pramocaine, also known as pramoxine or pramoxine hydrochloride, is a topical anesthetic that was discovered at Abbott Laboratories in 1953. It is primarily used as an antipruritic agent to relieve itching. Chemically, it is identified as p-n-butoxyphenyl gammamorpholinopropyl ether hydrochloride. During its research and development, pramoxine hydrochloride was found to be particularly effective among a group of alkoxy aryl alkamines as a topical local anesthetic. Pharmacological studies demonstrated that it is a potent agent with low acute and subacute toxicity. It is well-tolerated by most mucous membranes and has a low sensitizing potential in humans. Similar to other local anesthetics, pramoxine works by reducing the permeability of neuronal membranes to sodium ions. This action inhibits both the initiation and conduction of nerve impulses. Consequently, the processes of depolarization and repolarization in excitable neural membranes are blocked, resulting in localized numbness. Pramoxine hydrochloride is a key ingredient in popular over-the-counter products such as Gold Bond and Calamine Lotion, which are used to numb sensitive skin. It is also included in the pain relief variant of Neosporin and certain formulations of Sarna. The hydrochloride salt form of pramocaine is water-soluble, which enhances its usability in various topical applications. Topical anesthetics like pramocaine are commonly used to alleviate pain and itching caused by conditions such as sunburn, minor burns, insect bites or stings, poison ivy, poison oak, poison sumac, and minor cuts or scratches. Additionally, pramocaine and dibucaine are frequently found as active ingredients in over-the-counter hemorrhoid treatments.
